title: Normal form for symmetric polynomial additive two-cocycles
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] of prime characteristic $p>0$ [def-pc-field-characteristic]. Use polynomial rings [def-weil-polynomial-ring, def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. Define $c_p(X,Y)\in k[X,Y]$ to be the reduction of the integer polynomial $-\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}(\binom pj/p)X^jY^{p-j}$; the displayed integer coefficients are divided by $p$ before reduction to $k$. Let $f\in k[X,Y]$ satisfy $f(X,0)=f(0,Y)=0$, $f(X,Y)=f(Y,X)$, and
$$f(Y,Z)-f(X+Y,Z)+f(X,Y+Z)-f(X,Y)=0\quad\text{in }k[X,Y,Z].$$
There exist an integer $r\geq0$, elements $a_0,\ldots,a_r\in k$, and $b\in k[T]$ with $b(0)=0$ such that
$$f(X,Y)=\sum_{i=0}^{r}a_i c_p(X,Y)^{p^i}+b(X)+b(Y)-b(X+Y).$$
No perfection assumption on $k$ is required; $f=0$ is allowed, with all $a_i=0$ and $b=0$.

source.place: Lemma 15.26, printed p.316, with the symmetric cocycles and coboundaries of Proposition 15.10 and Corollary 15.11, printed pp.308-309. The assertion here is its existence clause written as an explicit polynomial identity, with the same sign for f_1=c_p.

proof.text: Write $\delta b=b(X)+b(Y)-b(X+Y)$. The polynomial definitions [def-weil-polynomial-ring, def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] give a finite decomposition $f=\sum_n f_n$, where $f_n$ is the sum of the monomials of total degree $n$. Normalization and symmetry hold separately for each $f_n$. Every substitution in the cocycle identity preserves total degree, so comparison of the degree-$n$ terms makes each $f_n$ a cocycle. Normalization kills the pure monomials, hence $f_0=f_1=0$. We prove by strong induction on $n$ that every such homogeneous cocycle has the required finite normal form, with $b(0)=0$. Degrees $0,1$ have the zero representation. In the remaining steps fix $n\geq2$ and write $h=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}u_iX^iY^{n-i}$, so symmetry says $u_i=u_{n-i}$.

source.place: Lemma 15.26, printed p.316, coefficient-identity argument; explicit agent-supplied detail, step 1.

proof.text:
Put $A=u_{n-1}$. For each $1\leq i\leq n-1$, compare the coefficient of $X^iY^{n-1-i}Z$ in the cocycle identity for $h$. The term $h(Y,Z)$ contributes zero because $i>0$, and $h(X,Y)$ contributes zero because the exponent of $Z$ is one. In $-h(X+Y,Z)$ only $-u_{n-1}(X+Y)^{n-1}Z$ contributes, giving $-A\binom{n-1}{i}$. In $h(X,Y+Z)$ the contribution is $(n-i)u_i$. Thus, in $k$,
$$(n-i)u_i=A\binom{n-1}{i}.\tag{*}$$
Here and below integers mean their images under $\mathbf Z\to k$ [def-pc-field-characteristic]; the binomial expansion follows by distributing the finite product of copies of $X+Y$ and counting which factors supply $X$.

source.place: Lemma 15.26, printed p.316, coefficient-identity argument; explicit agent-supplied detail, step 2.

proof.text:
If $p\nmid n$, the image of $n$ in $k$ is nonzero [def-pc-field-characteristic] and invertible [def-weil-field]. Apply (*) also at $n-i$ and use symmetry to obtain $iu_i=A\binom{n-1}{i-1}$. Adding the two identities gives $nu_i=A\binom ni$: the binomial coefficient counts subsets according to whether a fixed element belongs to them. Consequently
$$h=\frac{A}{n}\big((X+Y)^n-X^n-Y^n\big)=\delta\big(-\tfrac{A}{n}T^n\big).$$
This proves the inductive assertion in these degrees with every Witt coefficient zero and $b(0)=0$.

source.place: Lemma 15.26, printed p.316, coefficient-identity argument; explicit agent-supplied detail, step 3.

proof.text:
If $n=p$, put $d_i=\binom pi/p\in\mathbf Z$ for $1\leq i\leq p-1$. These are integers: $i!\binom pi=p(p-1)\cdots(p-i+1)$ is divisible by $p$, whereas $i!$ is prime to $p$. The integer identity $(p-i)d_i=\binom{p-1}{i}$ follows by writing out the factorials and cancelling before reduction. By (*) we have $(p-i)u_i=A(p-i)d_i$ in $k$. Since $1\leq p-i<p$, this factor is nonzero and invertible [def-pc-field-characteristic, def-weil-field], giving $u_i=Ad_i$. The sign in the statement's definition is therefore respected:
$$h=A\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}d_iX^iY^{p-i}=-A c_p(X,Y).$$
Take $a_0=-A$, all further coefficients zero, and $b=0$. This includes $p=2$, where $c_2=-XY$.

source.place: Lemma 15.26, printed p.316, coefficient-identity argument; explicit agent-supplied detail, step 4.

proof.text:
It remains to treat $p\mid n$ and $n>p$. The index $i=n-p$ lies between $1$ and $n-1$, so (*) gives $0=p u_{n-p}=A\binom{n-1}{p-1}$ in $k$. The latter binomial coefficient has image $1$: multiply it by $(p-1)!$ and use
$$(p-1)!\binom{n-1}{p-1}=\prod_{j=1}^{p-1}(n-j)\equiv\prod_{j=1}^{p-1}(-j)\pmod p.$$
The factor $(p-1)!$ is invertible in $k$, and $(-1)^{p-1}=1$ in $k$ (for $p=2$, $-1=1$). Hence $A=0$. Now (*) says $(n-i)u_i=0$. Whenever $p\nmid i$, also $p\nmid(n-i)$, so inversion forces $u_i=0$. Thus every surviving exponent of both variables is divisible by $p$. All cancellations used only the characteristic and field definitions [def-pc-field-characteristic, def-weil-field].

source.place: Lemma 15.26, printed p.316, coefficient-identity argument; explicit agent-supplied detail, step 5.

proof.text:
Set $m=n/p<n$ and define $g(U,V)=\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}u_{pj}U^jV^{m-j}$. The previous step gives $h(X,Y)=g(X^p,Y^p)$; $g$ is homogeneous of degree $m$, normalized and symmetric by its coefficients [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. For $0<j<p$, the same factorial argument as in step 4 gives $p\mid\binom pj$, so $(X+Y)^p=X^p+Y^p$ in characteristic $p$. Substitute $h=g(X^p,Y^p)$ in its cocycle equation. Its left side is the substitution $(U,V,W)=(X^p,Y^p,Z^p)$ in
$$g(V,W)-g(U+V,W)+g(U,V+W)-g(U,V).$$
This substitution is injective: distinct monomials $U^aV^bW^c$ map to distinct monomials $X^{pa}Y^{pb}Z^{pc}$, leaving their coefficients unchanged. Therefore the displayed polynomial is zero. This proves the cocycle hypothesis needed to apply the strong induction hypothesis to $g$.

source.place: Lemma 15.26, printed p.316, coefficient-identity argument; explicit agent-supplied detail, step 6.

proof.text:
By that induction hypothesis choose $g=\sum_{i=0}^{s}a_i c_p(U,V)^{p^i}+\delta b(U,V)$ with $b(0)=0$. Replacing $(U,V)$ by $(X^p,Y^p)$ gives
$$h=\sum_{i=0}^{s}a_i c_p(X,Y)^{p^{i+1}}+\delta\widetilde b(X,Y),\qquad \widetilde b(T)=b(T^p).$$
Indeed the binomial identity from step 6, iterated over finite sums, gives $c_p(X^p,Y^p)=c_p(X,Y)^p$: every coefficient of $c_p$ is an integer image, fixed by $z\mapsto z^p$ because this map is additive and sends $1$ to $1$. Also $b(X^p)+b(Y^p)-b(X^p+Y^p)=\widetilde b(X)+\widetilde b(Y)-\widetilde b(X+Y)$. Insert zero as the coefficient at index $0$, and note $\widetilde b(0)=0$. This closes the divisible-degree induction. Coefficients $a_i$ themselves were unchanged, so no surjectivity of Frobenius on $k$ was used.

source.place: Lemma 15.26, printed p.316, coefficient-identity argument; explicit agent-supplied detail, step 7.

proof.text: Apply the now-proved homogeneous assertion to the finitely many $f_n$ of step 1. Pad their finite coefficient lists by zeros to a common last index $r\geq0$, and add the lists and their polynomials $b_n$. Coefficientwise polynomial addition [def-weil-polynomial-ring, def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring] gives $a_i=\sum_n a_{n,i}$, $b=\sum_n b_n$, $b(0)=0$, and $f=\sum_{i=0}^{r}a_i c_p^{p^i}+\delta b$. For $f=0$, simply take $r=0$, $a_0=0$ and $b=0$. Every step worked in $k$ using only nonzero integer inverses, not roots of elements, so the stated absence of a perfection hypothesis is justified.

source.place: Lemma 15.26, printed p.316, coefficient-identity argument; explicit agent-supplied detail, step 8.
